title: Mecca Pact Binds Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan in Mutual Defense, Senate Passes Russia Sanctions, Kendall Clearance Revoked
subhead: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact in Mecca that treats an attack on any one as an attack on all — the most significant Sunni military alignment in decades. The US Senate overwhelmingly passed a Russia sanctions bill targeting energy buyers, and the Pentagon revoked former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall's security clearance over Air Force One disclosures.

sections.heading: Mecca Joint Defense Agreement Binds Three Sunni Powers
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Friday, stipulating that an armed attack against any of the three nations would be regarded as an attack on all. The pact was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accompanied by army chief General Asim Munir, according to the AP and NBC News.

A Turkish official described the agreement as purely defensive in nature, pledging mutual support only for defense, and said it was not directed against any specific actor and was open to other regional countries. The three nations share concerns about the increasingly aggressive military stances of both Israel and Iran, according to Reuters, and the agreement follows nearly a year of negotiations first reported in January.

Pakistan has already deployed about 8,000 troops, fighter jets, drones, and an air defense system to Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported in May. In 2023, Riyadh agreed to purchase Turkish drones in what Ankara called its largest defense export contract. The deal was sealed at Islam's holiest site — a deliberate choice that adds religious and political weight to a military arrangement. Analysts noted that while the pact builds on longstanding bilateral ties, it is unlikely to include a nuclear component, as Pakistan's deterrent remains focused on India, per Mansoor Ahmed of the Australian National University's Strategic and Defence Studies Centre.
sections.whyItMatters: Three of the Muslim world's most influential states are forming a collective defense architecture at a moment when the US security umbrella looks less reliable to Gulf partners — Saudi Arabia has been under Iranian-backed drone and missile fire for months with limited US protection. The pact's real test will be whether it translates into operational integration or remains symbolic.

sections.heading: Senate Passes Graham Russia Sanctions Bill 86-11
sections.body:
The US Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by a vote of 86 to 11 on Friday, according to NPR and the AP. The bill, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham who championed the legislation before his death last month, would sanction top Russian leaders and introduce penalties of up to 100% tariffs on nations purchasing Russian oil and natural gas — targeting major buyers like China and India. The bill also extends sanctions against Iran.

Graham's successor, Senator Darline Graham, said from the Senate floor: 'Without these profits the ability to fund the war would be crippled. This legislation hits Putin where it hurts.' The bill now heads to the House, where Speaker Mike Johnson has signaled support but faces a narrow margin. Some House Democrats have voiced opposition to granting Trump new tariff authorities.

India's Outlook India and Odisha TV flagged the bill's implications for New Delhi, noting it could impose up to 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian energy. The bill's passage represents one of the most significant congressional actions on Russia since the 2022 invasion, but its ultimate impact depends on House passage and presidential implementation.
sections.whyItMatters: If enacted, this bill would give the president extraordinary tariff authority over Russian energy trade, potentially disrupting flows to China and India worth billions. The 86-11 margin signals strong bipartisan resolve, but House passage is uncertain given Democratic concerns about tariff powers and Trump's transactional stance on Russia.

sections.heading: Pentagon Revokes Former Air Force Secretary Kendall's Security Clearance
sections.body:
The Pentagon revoked former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall's eligibility to access classified information and barred him from holding any sensitive position on Friday, alleging he disclosed sensitive information about Air Force One's capabilities to the media, the AP reported.

The revocation follows reporting in July, including by the New York Times, on security concerns over the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One, which lacked some of the advanced antimissile capabilities of its predecessor. Kendall was quoted in the Times saying the time for upgrades would not have been enough for 'all the normal Air Force One modifications' and expressing surprise that the plane was used outside the US.

Kendall told the AP he was 'completely mystified' by the revocation: 'I've always been extremely careful to not say anything classified, and as far as I know I have not. No one has said anything to me about what I'm asserted to have revealed.' The revocation, ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's department, makes Kendall the latest former defense official to lose clearance under the Trump administration. The move also sharpens scrutiny on the new Air Force One's actual security posture — the underlying story that prompted Kendall's comments.
sections.whyItMatters: Clearance revocations of former officials are unusual and signal an escalating pattern of the Trump administration using security-clearance powers punitively. More substantively, the episode highlights real concerns about the new Air Force One's defensive capabilities — concerns that the administration appears to be managing through leaker investigations rather than aircraft upgrades.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Ballistic Missile Interception Collapsed to 15% as Patriot Stocks Ran Out
sections.body:
Ukraine's Ministry of Defence published its official July air defense summary on August 7, confirming a devastating gap: Ukrainian forces intercepted about 87% of Shahed drones and cruise missiles but only 15% of ballistic missiles — stopping just 29 of 195 ballistic missiles Russia launched in July, according to the Tech Times analysis of official Ukrainian data.

The cause is specific and documented: Ukraine's supply of PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors — the only weapons capable of destroying Iskander-M ballistic missiles in terminal flight — was effectively exhausted around July 1, 2026. President Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine has been receiving approximately three times fewer anti-ballistic missiles than before in 2026. Air Force spokesperson Colonel Yurii Ihnat stated directly: 'To shoot down ballistic missiles, you need the assets to do so. We have enough systems, but what we need is a steady supply of missiles.'

The human cost is measurable: on July 6, Ukraine intercepted 326 UAVs and 37 of 39 cruise missiles — but zero ballistic missiles, resulting in at least 15 civilians killed in Kyiv alone. The UN confirmed July as the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022. Meanwhile, Ukraine's electronic warfare and drone-on-drone intercepts neutralized over 48,000 tactical-level drones in July — a layered defense winning the drone war while losing the ballistic one.
sections.whyItMatters: The 15% ballistic intercept rate versus 87% drone rate lays bare the Patriot interceptor shortage in operational terms. Every major ally is competing for the same limited PAC-3 MSE supply — and production lead times mean this gap will persist well into 2027 regardless of new orders.

sections.heading: Army Opens Five Test Ranges to Private Sector, Including Morocco
sections.body:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced Friday that the Army is opening five testing ranges to private defense companies — four in the US and one in partnership with Morocco — aiming to cut wait times from 12-18 months to 30 days, according to Stars and Stripes.

The domestic ranges are Dugway Proving Ground (Utah), West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground (Arizona), Camp Shelby (Mississippi), and Camp Grayling (Michigan). The fifth is the Multidomain Training Area range complex in Morocco, part of the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center (AMTEC). The ranges will test drones, counter-drone systems, long-range missiles, and low-cost air defense interceptors. The Army has launched a new website, testrange.army.mil, and assigned each company a 'concierge-esque' human point of contact, Driscoll said.

The move comes amid deepening concerns about munitions depletion from the Iran war. CNN reported this week that the US has used nearly 80% of its THAAD missile stockpile and about half its Patriot interceptors since the conflict began. The Army will host an event the week of September 13 at Camp Grayling simulating electronic warfare conditions currently seen in Ukraine to test drones and counter-drone systems, with quarterly events planned afterward.
sections.whyItMatters: Opening government ranges to private companies with 30-day turnaround is a structural shift in how the Pentagon approaches weapons development — compressing what was a 12-18 month booking process. The Morocco site is notable as the first overseas range offered for private-sector testing, reflecting both the urgency and the global scope of the munitions replenishment challenge.

sections.heading: Trump Threatens Jail for Munitions Leak Reports as Stockpile Debate Escalates
sections.body:
President Trump vowed on Truth Social Thursday to seek 'long-term jail sentences' for officials who leaked information about US munitions stockpiles, calling the disclosures 'treasonous.' The Washington Post reported that Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about munitions shortfalls at Camp David last week, though the White House and Pentagon denied the confrontation occurred.

Trump posted: 'The U.S. has massive amounts of 'munitions,' especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country's history.' He called the Post's reporting 'treasonous.' The administration's $87.6 billion supplemental budget request, sent to Congress in June, includes $18 billion to replace Patriot interceptors, Tomahawks, and THAAD missiles, according to Time.

Meanwhile, Iranian Defense Minister Majid Ibn-e-Reza posted on X: 'Each day, the signs of the enemy's diminishing capabilities become increasingly evident.' The public dimension of this dispute — a president threatening criminal prosecution for leaks about classified stockpile data — represents an escalation in the administration's approach to managing information about the war's material costs.
sections.whyItMatters: The clash between leaked assessments showing severe depletion and the administration's insistence that stocks are adequate is now a political crisis in its own right. Threatening leak prosecutions while simultaneously requesting $18 billion in interceptor replacements is a tension that congressional debate over the supplemental will force into the open.

sections.heading: Senate Russia Sanctions Bill Targets India and China Energy Trade
sections.body:
Beyond its domestic significance, the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act would give the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian energy — chiefly China and India, which have been the primary buyers of Russian crude since the invasion. The bill also extends sanctions against Iran.

India's Outlook India and Rediff highlighted the potential impact on New Delhi, which has purchased discounted Russian crude throughout the war, refining it for export. The bill's tariff mechanism could effectively force India to choose between access to Russian energy and the US market — a dilemma that has sharpened as India-US trade negotiations are already underway.

The bill still faces a House vote after the August recess. Speaker Mike Johnson has signaled support, but some House Democrats oppose granting Trump broad tariff authority. The bill passed the Senate with bipartisan support, including from the late Senator Graham's sister, who now holds his seat and argued from the floor that Russia's war is 'primarily funded by the revenue Russia rakes in from energy sales.'
sections.whyItMatters: This bill would weaponize US market access to squeeze Russian energy revenue at source — but only if the House passes it and the president enforces it. The India-China dimension makes this a global trade confrontation, not just a Russia sanctions measure. If enacted and enforced, it could reshape energy trade flows that have sustained Russia's war economy.

bottomLine: The Mecca defense pact creates a new Sunni military axis that could reshape Middle East security arrangements if it moves beyond symbolism — something Pakistan's 8,000 troops already in Saudi Arabia suggest it might. In Washington, the Senate's 86-11 vote on Russia sanctions puts congressional pressure on the White House to confront Russian and Iranian energy revenue, while Trump's threats to jail officials who leaked munitions data underscore the political volatility of the Iran war's material costs. Ukraine's 15% ballistic intercept rate reveals in stark numbers what Patriot shortages mean on the ground, and the Army's decision to open test ranges — including one in Morocco — to private firms with 30-day turnaround signals how urgently the Pentagon wants to accelerate weapons development. The day's events circle a common theme: the gap between munitions demand and supply is reshaping alliances, laws, and institutional norms faster than production lines can catch up.
sources: AP News, NBC News, Reuters, NPR, Time, Tech Times, Stars and Stripes, Breaking Defense, AP (Kendall), Washington Post, Al Jazeera, Anadolu Agency, Daily Sabah, Outlook India, The New Arab, Janes, Aviation Week, Interesting Engineering
